hostSurfaces.purpose: A host is not one uniform capability target. Codex CLI, the Codex IDE extension and the ChatGPT desktop app are the same registered host reading the same ~/.codex config, but they do NOT expose the same tools -- routing a task to the built-in Browser succeeds on one and silently has nowhere to go on another. This records which surface actually offers which capability, so a skill can request an outcome and resolve a provider instead of naming a tool that may not exist where it runs.
hostSurfaces.modelNote: Deliberately NOT modelled as extra entries in registry/agents.json. Hosts are split there when their surfaces read DIFFERENT paths -- antigravity-ide and cursor-agent each have their own config file, which is what earns them a host entry. Every Claude surface reads ~/.claude and every Codex surface reads ~/.codex, so splitting them would duplicate 11 and 12 capability mappings that deploy to identical destinations and add nothing. What differs is capability availability, and that lives here.

capabilityMeanings.browser.isolated: A first-party browser the agent drives itself, with its own profile. Suits localhost and public pages; carries no signed-in session.
capabilityMeanings.browser.authenticated: A browser using the user's real profile, so already-signed-in sites work. Requires a live extension connection, not merely an installed product.
capabilityMeanings.computer.gui: First-party control of native desktop applications.

surfaces.verification: learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser states verbatim: 'Browser isn't available in Codex CLI or the Codex IDE extension. Open the ChatGPT desktop app to use the built-in browser.' MCP remains available on this surface, so structured integrations are the route here, not browser automation.
Same documented sentence as codex-cli names the IDE extension explicitly.

The same page states Browser is available in ChatGPT on the web and in the ChatGPT desktop app. The Chrome-extension and Computer Use surfaces were not probed from this machine, so they are recorded null rather than assumed.

browser.isolated measured live: the in-app Browser pane opened and navigated. browser.authenticated measured FALSE: list_connected_browsers returned an empty array, so Claude in Chrome is not connected on this machine -- the product exists but the capability does not, which is exactly the distinction this table is for. computer.gui is available, with documented tier limits: browsers are read-only and terminals/IDEs reject typing, so it cannot substitute for either browser capability.

hostSurfaces.note: null means not established, never 'assumed false'. A false must carry evidence in the same entry, the same rule registry/mcps.json applies to protocol revisions. Enforced by tests/Test-HostSurfaces.ps1.

notes: OAuth consent and provider login remain provider-controlled.
